extracted.intended_audience: Writers Guild members; professional screenwriters and long-form television writers (and their agents/representatives)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of contractual creative rights, protections, and recommended negotiation strategies under the WGA Theatrical and Television Basic Agreement (MBA) for writers of theatrical motion pictures and long-form television. Covers pre-development through post-production rights, credits, separated rights, registration, indemnification, and enforcement procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working Only for Signatories (Working Rule 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's rights are created and protected by the contract that governs his or her work. Working Rule 8 requires members to work for and sell or option literary material only to companies that have signed a collective bargaining agreement with the Guild.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures writers are covered by Guild agreements and enforcement mechanisms. Writers should avoid deals with non-signatories to preserve contractual protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Minimum Basic Agreement (MBA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MBA is the industry-wide collective bargaining agreement that sets the minimum terms for options, purchases, and employment of writers for theatrical motion pictures and television programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MBA is the baseline; individual contracts cannot undercut it but may improve upon most terms (except credit determination, which is governed by the MBA and Credits Manuals). Consult the MBA text for details where ambiguity exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual Contract — Ability to Improve on MBA
rubrics_metrics.description: Every hire, sale, license or option should be covered by a deal memo or contract; writers may negotiate provisions that improve on the MBA (overscale), except that writing credit determination remains subject to the MBA and Credits Manuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the MBA as incorporated reference in individual deals and negotiate overscale creative rights, publicity placement, and compensation where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overscale Creative Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers and their representatives may negotiate above-scale (overscale) creative rights in individual contracts to secure greater involvement or protections than the MBA minimums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although historically harder to obtain than overscale pay, overscale creative provisions often cost little and can be negotiated (e.g., more rewrites, guaranteed participation). The Guild encourages seeking these improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: PBS Agreement as Enhanced Rights Model
rubrics_metrics.description: The WGA Public TV Freelance Agreement (PBS Agreement) provides enhanced creative rights for public television writers and can serve as a model for negotiating enhanced rights in non-PBS contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may negotiate to incorporate PBS creative rights into other contracts or elect among PBS provisions depending on bargaining position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright Ownership and Registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright vests initially with the creator (five exclusive rights listed). Registration with the U.S. Copyright Office secures legal enforcement; WGA Registration establishes possession on a date for plagiarism disputes but is not a substitute for U.S. Copyright registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers own scripts created on spec; hired scripts may be 'work for hire' vesting copyright with employer. When possible, register with both WGA and U.S. Copyright Office; understand typical U.S. industry practice of transferring copyright on sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractual construct in the MBA that returns certain rights (publication, stage dramatic rights, sequel payments, reacquisition rights) to the original writer even after copyright transfer to a company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separated Rights can include reacquisition windows, sequel/merchandising/publication rights and vary by theatrical vs television; a full treatment is available in a Guild pamphlet. Writers should seek separated rights where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who Gets Separated Rights (professional writer definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Separated Rights apply to original literary material covered by the MBA when the writer meets the MBA's technical definition of a 'professional writer' (theatrical/TV credit, 13 weeks industry employment, produced play, or published novel), or negotiates to be treated as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers who do not meet the technical definition may attempt to negotiate professional status or separated rights into their individual contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration of Literary Material with the Guild (WGA Registration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guild operates a registration service to record the date of registration for concepts, stories, treatments and scripts for a fee (member/non-member rates) to help in authorship disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best to register material before circulation. WGA registration provides a Guild witness if needed in disputes but does not replace official Copyright Office registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of Professional Status of Writers (Article 48)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 48 of the MBA establishes many creative rights and created the Committee on the Professional Status of Writers to study and recommend improvements; strengthened since 1988 with further gains in 1995, 1998 and 2001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 48 fosters writer inclusion across pre-production, production, post-production, and marketing; writers should reference Article 48 in negotiations and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on the Dissemination of Script Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless a company has optioned or purchased literary material, it may not disseminate critiques or synopses of the material outside the company without writer consent, except to entities with a business relationship to the company (Article 60).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should avoid consenting to broad circulation privileges and should insist on first seeing any coverage before approving further dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on Shopping Material (television and feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MBA allows writers to restrict in writing the extent to which a company may 'shop' speculative material; violations require payment to the writer through the Guild of $750 per party to whom the script was improperly submitted (Article 49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should put shopping limits in writing; for television, written consent in a separate document is required before a company may shop unacquired material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to the First Rewrite of Optioned Material (features and TV)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MBA guarantees the writer of an original screenplay or teleplay the right to perform the first rewrite under employment during the option period unless waived in writing (Article 16.A.3.d. and 16.B.3.i.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should not casually waive this right; as an overscale negotiation, seek additional guaranteed rewrites or rights to all rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to the First Rewrite After Acquisition or License
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer who sells or options an original screenplay must be offered the first rewrite unless unable or voluntarily waives the right. For long teleplays, similar protections apply with timing exceptions (Article 16.A.3.c.; 16.B.3.h.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waivers must be given freely and not as boilerplate; writers should insist on meeting with company representatives if replacement is contemplated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrites of Original Material Written Under Employment (meeting requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the company chooses to replace the first writer, the company must meet with that writer (senior production executive who has read the material) and give the writer an opportunity to discuss continuing on the project (Article 16.A.3.c., 16.B.3.h.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meetings must occur in sufficient time for discussion; writers should seek the stronger sold-or-optioned rewrite protections as an overscale improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to Perform Revisions After New or Changed Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: For original material sold or licensed by a professional writer, the MBA guarantees additional revisions if a new/changed element (e.g., director, principal performer) is committed. The writer must be offered first opportunity; this obligation expires three years after delivery of the first writer's first or final set of revisions, whichever is later (Article 16.A.3.c.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers are encouraged to negotiate extension or elimination of the three-year limitation and to secure guaranteed revisions in television when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation About Requested Revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers or creative executives are required to consult with the writer to discuss each set of revisions requested (Article 16.A.3.e., 16.B.3.j.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents notes being sent without explanation; as an overscale, specify which executive must consult in the individual contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization of Rewrites (deal memo naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must include in a writer's deal memo or contract the name(s) of person(s authorized to request rewrites or receive delivery of drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects writers against demands for free rewrites and clarifies who may authorize work and payment obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-form Television Rewrite Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a writer agrees to do three revisions and negotiates compensation, the producer may request/receive revisions before submission to the network; writer is paid for first draft to producer. Signatories to the Network MBA must notify the network when the first draft is received; AMPTP MBA signatories promise timely payment and licensee receives one less draft (Article 13.B.7.f. and AMPTP Sideletter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should confirm network/payment arrangements and ask if the network has agreed to pay for drafts the network doesn't receive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweepstakes Pitching (disclosure of approximate competitors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 2001 MBA, if a writer asks whether others have been invited to pitch/interview, the company must tell the writer the approximate number of writers invited; on long-form TV the company must make best efforts to inform at invitation time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides transparency during competitive pitch situations; writers should ask about the number of invitees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice to Writers on the Same Material
rubrics_metrics.description: The MBA obligates a company to notify each writer of other writers currently employed on the same television project and previously employed writers; in features, the company must provide this information upon request (Article 18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows writers to know who else is working on the material and to be informed when subsequent writers are employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script Cover Pages (naming prior and current writers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Until final credits are determined, the cover page must include the name of the first writer followed by 'revisions' and the names/dates of subsequent writers. Subsequent writers should mark 'current revisions by' and not remove earlier writers' names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover pages reflect those who worked on drafts (not final credit). Final credits are determined separately by the Guild.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script Annotations for Feature and Television Scripts
rubrics_metrics.description: If script annotations will be required for fact-based or fact-inspired scripts, the company must inform the writer at negotiation and provide company guidelines or standards (Article 13.A.18. and 13.B.11.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should negotiate time periods and additional compensation for annotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warranty and Indemnification Protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The MBA requires companies to cover writers on their errors and omissions (E&O) insurance and to indemnify writers against damages and legal expenses for claims involving material supplied by the company, material incorporated by the company, changes made at company request, or material not furnished by the writer (Article 28).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When indemnification is required, the company must pay attorney's fees, travel expenses, copying costs, and the writer must cooperate in defense without incurring costs. Writers should ensure these protections are in their contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited Burdensome Indemnity Clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: The MBA forbids clauses that: require writers to forfeit objection to contributing to settlement costs; require indemnification for material other than that furnished by the writer; require indemnification for defamation/privacy/publicity unless writer knowingly violated rights or was asked to use an actual person and answered risk questions; and (new in 2001) require indemnification for an 'alleged breach' (an actual breach must be established).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should resist insertion of these forbidden clauses into individual contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Producer Meetings (pre-production involvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: For theatrical motion pictures, pilots, movies-of-the-week and miniseries, if no director engaged, the company will arrange a pre-production meeting between the producer and the writer (or a participating writer of the company's choice) for a meaningful discussion of translating the writer's vision to screen (Article 48.A.1.; 48.A.2.; 48.A.3.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The meeting covers tone, location, casting, director choice, etc. Writers should request these meetings and negotiate for greater participation if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director Meetings (writer-director collaboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2001 MBA expresses a preferred practice that shortly after assignment, the director meet with the writer (or previous writer of director's choice) prior to any decision to hire a new writer; for long-form TV the executive producer and director should meet with the writer to share creative views (Writer-Director Collaboration Appendices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages early director-writer collaboration and communication; writers should reference the applicable Collaboration Appendix in negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call Sheets and Staff Directories / Crew Lists
rubrics_metrics.description: On features and long-form television, the company must list up to three writers or writing teams on the call sheet adjacent to the director/producer(s). The currently employed writer will be provided a copy of the daily call sheet. All participating writers will be listed in staff directories/crew lists (Article 48.B. and 48.C.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These listings increase visibility and acknowledgment of writers on set and in production materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast Readings (invitation and private comment protocol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred practice: the director invite the currently employed writer to the first cast reading (theatrical) or executive producer/director invite the writer (long-form TV). When attending, writer comments should be made privately to the director (and executive producer if present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should express desire to attend; maintain private commentary protocol for constructive collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set Visits (right to request)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2001 MBA preferred practice: if a writer requests, the company will arrange a set visit at an appropriate time and allow a reasonable number of guests; the director may approve or deny visits for confidentiality, cast dynamics, or other reasons (Writer-Director Collaboration Appendices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should coordinate visits with the company and director and negotiate set visit rights/expenses in contracts if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location Expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: If the company requires a writer to travel for project work, the company must provide first class travel, board and lodging (Article 21). Additional writing services authorized on location must be compensated; expenses are reimbursed as authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should negotiate travel and per diem terms and compensation for authorized work while on location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual Negotiations for Expanded Participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies invite writers to express desire for more involvement; individual contracts may establish greater, specific involvement (absolute right to be present on set, paid expenses, presence at rehearsals, viewing dailies, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate explicit language referencing Article 48 and appropriate Collaboration Appendix to secure expanded, enforceable participation rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: PBS: Consultation with Writer (casting, locale, director)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PBS Agreement requires the company to 'consult with the writer in good faith as to decisions regarding casting of principal performers and choice of principal locale and director' and to give reasonable access to the director for consultations regarding interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These PBS provisions can be sought as overscale improvements in other contracts to increase writer influence on major creative decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PBS: Consultation Regarding Script Changes (pre/post/principal photography)
rubrics_metrics.description: PBS requires greater writer participation in script changes: during pre/post production changes are made 'in consultation with the writer' if present or available by phone; during principal photography the writer must have the first opportunity to make changes if present or available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate for specification of consultation procedures and compensation for additional script-change work.

rubrics_metrics.name: PBS: Notice of Rehearsal Dates and Production Schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: PBS specifies that the company 'shall give notice to the writer sufficiently in advance of all rehearsal dates and scheduled dates for production' so the writer can be present if desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek similar scheduling notice in non-PBS contracts to enable participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: PBS: Viewing Dailies
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the PBS Agreement the writer has the right to view dailies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viewing dailies can be important for creative input; writers should negotiate for this right when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast/Crew Events (post-production participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2001 MBA provides that all participating writers on theatrical and long-form motion pictures be invited to cast/crew events; the company is not required to provide transportation/overnight accommodations unless specified (Article 48.B. and 48.C.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should negotiate for travel/accommodation coverage and guest invitations if attendance is expected/valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewing Cuts (writer's viewing period and director's cut rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: All participating writers have the right to view a cut of the film. For theatrical motion pictures, each participating writer has a 'Writer's Viewing Period' scheduled so suggestions may be implemented if approved. For movies-of-the-week/miniseries, the company must invite writers to view the director's cut within 48 hours following the company's viewing; videocassette substitution is allowed in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should seek clear scheduling terms for viewing periods and request videocopies when in-person viewing is impracticable; participation in discussion meetings is required to be offered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attending Sneak Previews
rubrics_metrics.description: Credited writers of theatrical films, television pilots, movies-of-the-week and miniseries must be invited to the first sneak preview if held in Los Angeles County. If possible, company must give credited writers five days notice (Article 48.B. and 48.C.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inadvertent failure due to exigency is not a breach, so writers should proactively ask about sneak preview timing and request invitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attending the Premiere, Press Junkets and Festivals
rubrics_metrics.description: Credited writer(s) of a theatrical motion picture will be invited to attend the domestic premiere or domestic festival where the film is first exhibited, unless notified otherwise. Company will furnish transportation/accommodations if travel exceeds 150 miles (Article 21 and Article 48.B.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should negotiate guarantees for invitations, company coverage of costs for writer and guest(s), and parity in travel arrangements compared to other credited writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Videocassette Copies (home video copies to writers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The company must furnish, at no cost, credited writers of a theatrical motion picture with a videocassette of the movie when videocassettes are made (Article 48.B.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With evolving formats, seek parity for DVD/Blu-ray/digital screeners and inclusion in distribution materials where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy of the Shooting Script
rubrics_metrics.description: Participating writers are entitled to a copy (or two copies in some instances) of the final shooting script (Article 13.B.8.f., Theatrical Schedule A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure contract reflects entitlement to final shooting script copies for writers' records and future use as permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-Screen Credit (Guild determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies signatory to the MBA agree to abide by the Guild's determination of writing credits in accordance with the credits schedules of the MBA (Article 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-screen credit placement, sequence, and publicity appearance follow Guild-determined credits rather than unilateral company decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of the Writing Credit
rubrics_metrics.description: MBA generally requires writing credit be placed next to the director: in main titles the writing credit appears on a title card immediately preceding the director's card and no more than second credit before start; in end titles it appears immediately following the director as the second card (Theatrical Schedule A, para 8; Television Schedule A, para 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should confirm placement expectations in contracts and consider negotiating more prominent treatment in publicity materials even beyond MBA minima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a Pseudonym
rubrics_metrics.description: Credited writers of theatrical motion pictures may use a 'reasonable' pseudonym if requested within five business days after credits are final and if paid less than $200,000. In television, similar pseudonym rights exist tied to protest timing and compensation thresholds (Television Schedule A, para 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an overscale improvement, negotiate higher compensation ceilings or absolute pseudonym rights regardless of compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit in Advertising and Publicity (parity and inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MBA generally requires WGA-determined writing credits to appear in advertising and publicity in parity with the director or producer. The 2001 MBA enhanced appearance of writing credits in press kits, laserdiscs/DVDs and requires identity/background/filmography of credited writers in standard print/electronic press kits if director information is included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies must interview credited writers for EPK inclusion if director is interviewed (company retains discretion to include material). Writers should submit filmography at last delivery for publicity inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessive Credits (Guild objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MBA preamble highlights the Guild's objection to possessive credits (e.g., 'A Film by'), which the Guild believes denigrates collaborative authorship; issue unresolved industry-wide and remains subject for further advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and representatives should voice opposition to possessive credits in negotiations and industry discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee on the Professional Status of Writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Two Committees on the Professional Status of Writers (theatrical and long-form TV) created in Article 48 meet at least three times per year; joint company and Guild committees study creative rights and professional status and publish recommended standards of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may provide input via WGA Member Services or WGAE's Executive Director to influence the Committee's agenda and recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint WGA-DGA Creative Rights Committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Three joint WGA-DGA committees (theatrical, long-form, episodic) established to further collegial writer-director relations; meet twice a year plus an additional CEOs meeting; discuss Writer-Director Collaboration issues (meetings, cast reading attendance, set visits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These committees produce guidelines and joint initiatives to improve collaboration between writers and directors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Initiatives to Enhance Writer-Director Collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreed initiatives include annual magazine issues on successful collaborations, joint seminars, and a pamphlet setting forth creative rights of writers and directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should monitor and participate in these initiatives to promote best practices and collaboration models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future Negotiations Clause (protection of creative rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2001 MBA provides that each Company agrees it will not negotiate a provision in any collective bargaining agreement that infringes upon the creative rights of the writer under the WGA MBA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clause aims to preserve negotiated creative rights in future agreements industry-wide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract Enforcement by the Guild
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guild assists writers in enforcing contract provisions, including creative rights, at no cost to the writer other than dues. Claims Departments pursue violations and Guild Legal takes disputes to binding arbitration when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should promptly report violations to enable timely action and possible resolution via Guild channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hotline Option for Article 48 Violations
rubrics_metrics.description: A hotline between the Guild and companies is the first resort for certain Article 48 disputes; if no resolution within seven days of the Guild's initial contact, the Guild may arbitrate arbitrable disputes. Guild will first try to secure writer participation rather than damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call WGAW Creative Rights Dept. or WGAE attorneys and identify the issue as a 'creative rights problem' for expedited handling; this is designed for quick, informal resolution when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance and Arbitration (legal escalation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When hotline/settlement fails, the Guild arbitrates claims; legal staff prepares cases, conducts arbitrations, and many cases settle before hearing. Cases are funded by member dues (no individual cost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should try to secure additional arbitration rights in individual contracts (e.g., make certain hotline-subject provisions arbitrable). Contact Claims or Contracts Departments promptly to preserve deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact and Enforcement Channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific contact points and phone numbers are provided for queries about contract provisions, claims, and enforcement (WGAW and WGAE phone numbers listed for Contracts, Claims, Creative Rights and Legal Departments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure where to go, call WGAW Creative Rights Dept. or WGAE for guidance; do not delay reporting known violations because contractual deadlines may bar action.
